source_text: I'm a bit frustrated that line 282 et seq. of *claude-repl:claude-2* describes a speed fix for the Python that proved that turned out not to be workable.  My idea of porting the project to LISP and getting a speedup that way also proved impractical. I'd like to check: had we *started* this project in Common Lisp and generated Python, could we have gotten speedups?

fragments.text: I'm a bit frustrated that line 282 et seq.
of *claude-repl:claude-2* describes a speed fix for the Python that proved that turned out not to be workable.
My idea of porting the project to LISP and getting a speedup that way also proved impractical.
I'd like to check: had we *started* this project in Common Lisp and generated Python, could we have gotten speedups?

reply_text:
㊥ ("could we have gotten speedups?") Probably yes, but less than you'd hope. A compiler written natively in Common Lisp would run its own work several times faster than the Python port, and the generated Python would cost almost nothing, since running it took 8.5 s of a 2,314 s cold probe. Language doesn't touch the larger costs, though: the Lean parsing in native code, a parse of nearly the whole repository on every cold run, and finding which elaborator step goes wrong one probe at a time. My rough guess is that a cold check would have shrunk from about 30 minutes to somewhere in the 5–15 minute range. Nothing here has measured that.

🈖 (why the Lisp port was slow) The Lisp port didn't fail because of Lisp. It translated Python into Lisp, so it had to rebuild Python's object model on top of Lisp. Every field read went through generic string-keyed attribute lookup and generic call dispatch. bench2 (`/tmp/pyreg/lisp/bench2/README.md`) made three targeted fixes and was still 25–31x slower, with the cost spread across the whole object model rather than a few hot spots. Lisp written natively from the start would use typed structs and direct calls, and would avoid that cost. Your counterfactual is also the easier direction to translate in. Restricted Lisp (structs, functions, no metaobject tricks) maps into Python without trouble. Python mapped into Lisp has to carry descriptors, the method resolution order (MRO) and `__getattr__` along with it.

㊢ (where a cold probe's time goes) codex's cProfile of a cold `pushSyntax` run (`/tmp/pyreg/lisp/cold1/README.md`):

| Phase | Seconds (inclusive, overlapping) | Would Lisp change it? |
|---|---:|---|
| Lean parsing + flat-syntax decode | 741 (361 of it in LeanPy's native wrapper) | Only the Python half |
| Repository-wide semantic inventory (re-parses 2,049 of 2,209 `.lean` files) | 641 | No. It's a design choice |
| Owner-index access (456,650 calls) | 649 | Partly. A disk-cache cost |
| Payload validation (50M `dataclasses.fields` calls) | 339 | Mostly gone. That's the Python object model |
| Pickle writes | 119 | Gone in an image |
| Running the generated code | 8.5 | Irrelevant |

The CPU-bound Python work would speed up. The native parser and the broad inventory wouldn't.

🈖 (the line-282 fix) The bigger difference is the one you were after with the warm image. A Lisp project would probably never have built the on-disk object cache with compiler fingerprints, because the image itself holds that state. The resident-process idea from that passage failed because of that disk cache. `/tmp/pyreg/overnight/resident-verdict.md` found that a failed first call wrote partial results into the shared cache, so the second call started from a different state and gave a different verdict. That's a defect in the cache design, not a Python limit. Lisp has its own version of the risk: data that the old definition of a function computed stays in the image after you redefine it. Your rule that the image is for searching and a cold run is the check would still hold. It would just be cheaper to follow.

㊟ (what wouldn't change) The overnight fixes kept turning out to be pieces of Lean's term elaborator: expected-type propagation, instance order, implicit metavariables, erasure. Most of the time went into finding which step diverged, and each attempt cost one probe. A faster language makes each attempt cheaper but doesn't reduce the number of them. A diff of the port's elaborated terms against Lean's (S4, now with codex-23) attacks that count, and that would have been needed in either language.

㊟ (the condition on all this) This assumes the compiler itself could have been in Lisp, with only its output in Python. If Rob's mission requires the compiler to be Python (mfuton-share is a Python codebase, and the mission has a "do not start from scratch" gate), then CL→Python would mean transpiling the whole compiler. The output would be at least as slow as hand-written Python, and the gain would be limited to iterating in the image.
